nameStory: Drummond's phlox honors Scottish botanist Thomas Drummond, who collected this colorful wildflower during his adventurous 1833-1835 expedition to Texas. Drummond sent seeds and specimens of this stunning plant back to Britain, where gardeners fell in love with its vibrant blooms. The name 'phlox' comes from the Greek word for 'flame,' perfectly capturing the fiery colors of these eye-catching flowers.
description: Drummond's phlox is a cheerful annual wildflower that brings splashes of brilliant color to gardens and roadsides. This compact plant typically grows 6-18 inches tall with a bushy, spreading habit. Its five-petaled flowers bloom in dense, rounded clusters and come in an amazing rainbow of colors - from pure white and soft pink to deep purple, bright red, and even nearly black. Originally from Texas, this heat-loving beauty has spread throughout the southeastern United States and occasionally pops up in New England gardens.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Five flat, round petals form perfect star-shaped flowers about 1 inch across, clustered in dense, dome-shaped heads. The petals feel papery-thin and often have a sweet, honey-like fragrance that's strongest in the evening.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves grow opposite each other along the stem, feeling slightly rough and fuzzy to the touch. The leaves are typically 1-3 inches long with smooth edges and prominent veins.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms neat, mounded clumps with multiple branching stems that feel somewhat sticky when handled. The plant has a compact, bushy appearance that spreads wider than it is tall.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, three-chambered seed capsules that split open when ripe, releasing tiny brown seeds. The dried capsules make a subtle rattling sound when shaken.

habitat: In New England, Drummond's phlox is extremely rare in the wild, with only three recorded observations. When found, it's typically an escaped garden plant growing along roadsides, in disturbed soils, or in sunny, well-drained areas. This heat-loving southern species prefers sandy or rocky soils and full sun exposure.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate as soil warms, and young plants develop their characteristic narrow leaves and branching structure.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season brings masses of colorful flowers from early to late summer, with the sweetest fragrance in the evenings when moths are active pollinators.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue into early fall, followed by seed capsule formation. As an annual, the entire plant dies with the first hard frost.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts survive the winter, though seeds may remain dormant in the soil until spring warmth triggers germination.

funFact: Drummond's phlox flowers actually change their fragrance throughout the day - they're nearly scentless in bright sunlight but release their sweetest, most intoxicating perfume at dusk to attract night-flying moths as pollinators!
confusionNotes: In gardens, Drummond's phlox might be confused with other phlox species, but its annual nature (dies completely each year) and compact, mounded growth habit set it apart from perennial cousins. Remember: if it's short, bushy, and doesn't come back next year, it's likely Drummond's phlox rather than the taller, perennial garden phlox.
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'annual phlox,' this plant can sometimes behave as a short-lived perennial in very mild climates, leading to confusion about its true nature. In New England's harsh winters, however, it's strictly annual and quite rare outside of cultivation.
compareHints: Unlike its New England relatives, Drummond's phlox is an annual that must be replanted each year, while fall phlox, moss phlox, and blue phlox are all perennials that return yearly. Drummond's phlox also has the most diverse color range and the most compact, mounded growth habit of any phlox species. Its flowers are typically smaller and more densely clustered than those of the tall fall phlox but larger than the tiny blooms of creeping moss phlox.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Fall phlox is much taller and more robust than its low-growing cousins like moss phlox and creeping phlox, which form ground-hugging mats.
Unlike its taller relatives like fall phlox which can grow 3-4 feet tall with large flower clusters, moss phlox stays low to the ground.
Among New England phloxes, creeping phlox is unique in its woodland habitat and creeping growth habit.
Blue phlox differs from its garden cousin fall phlox by being much shorter, blooming in spring rather than late summer, and having a more open flower cluster.
